name: Aquila
title: Tentmaker and co-worker of Paul
summary: Originally from Pontus on the Black Sea, Aquila was a Jewish believer who, together with his wife Priscilla, was expelled from Rome when Emperor Claudius ordered the expulsion of Jews around 49 AD. The couple settled in Corinth, where they shared both their home and tentmaking workshop with the apostle Paul. Over the years, Aquila and Priscilla became among Paul's most trusted coworkers – they accompanied him to Ephesus, guided the eloquent Apollos into a deeper understanding of the gospel, and opened their home as a gathering place for believers in several cities. Paul commends them for having risked their lives on his behalf and calls them his fellow workers in Christ Jesus, which testifies to the great trust and love between them.

keyEvents.title: Expelled from Rome
keyEvents.description: Aquila and Priscilla had to leave Rome when Emperor Claudius expelled the Jews, probably around 49 AD.

keyEvents.title: Tentmaker with Paul in Corinth
keyEvents.description: Paul lived and worked with Aquila and Priscilla in Corinth because they shared the same trade as tentmakers.

keyEvents.title: To Ephesus with Paul
keyEvents.description: Aquila and Priscilla followed Paul to Ephesus and stayed there to continue the work.

keyEvents.title: Teaching of Apollos
keyEvents.description: Aquila and Priscilla took care of Apollos and explained the way of God more accurately to him.

keyEvents.title: House church at Aquila and Priscilla's home
keyEvents.description: The couple hosted house churches, both in Ephesus and later in Rome, showing their central role in early Christian networks.

keyEvents.title: Risked their lives for Paul
keyEvents.description: Paul wrote that Aquila and Priscilla had risked their own lives for his sake, and that all Gentile-Christian churches owed them thanks.

keyEvents.title: Greeting in Paul's last letter
keyEvents.description: In what is considered one of Paul's last letters, he sends greetings to Priscilla and Aquila, testifying to their lasting importance and close relationship with the apostle.

versions.summary: Aquila was a Jewish-Christian man from Pontus, married to Priscilla. They were expelled from Rome under Emperor Claudius and settled in Corinth, where they welcomed Paul. As tentmakers, they worked together with Paul. They were trusted coworkers who risked their lives for Paul and led house churches.

versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Tentmaker and Leader' is clear, but could be more descriptive. 'Tentmaker and Church Leader' or 'Tentmaker and Co-worker with Paul' provides more context. Suggesting 'Tentmaker and Co-worker with Paul' to better reflect his role in the NT.; [major] Aquila was explicitly a tentmaker (Acts 18:3), and this is an important part of his identity. The role 'tentmaker' should be included. In addition, he taught (along with Priscilla) Apollos in the faith (Acts 18:26), so 'teacher' or 'mentor' could be considered. He also hosted a house church (1 Cor 16:19, Rom 16:5), so 'church leader' is more precise than just 'leader'.; [minor] 'Disciple' is a general term. 'Co-worker' (as Paul calls him in Rom 16:3) would have been more precise and biblically grounded.; [major] An important event is missing: Aquila and Priscilla instructed Apollos more accurately about the way of God (Acts 18:26). This is a central event in their ministry.; [minor] The house church at Aquila and Priscilla's home is mentioned in 1 Cor 16:19 and Rom 16:5. This is an important part of their ministry and should be included as a key event.; [major] There are no footnotes. Several interesting historical and theological details should be covered, including the expulsion under Claudius, the order Priscilla/Aquila in NT texts, and their role as hosts of house churches.

footnotes.text: The Roman historian Suetonius mentions the expulsion of Jews from Rome under Emperor Claudius (ca. 49 AD) and notes unrest related to "Chrestus," which many scholars believe is a reference to Christ. This may indicate that there were conflicts in the Jewish synagogues in Rome connected to Christian preaching.

In several New Testament texts, Priscilla (Prisca) is mentioned before Aquila (Acts 18:18, 26; Rom 16:3; 2 Tim 4:19). This is unusual in antiquity and has led scholars to discuss whether Priscilla may have had a more prominent role in the couple, either socially, spiritually, or both.

House churches were the most common form of Christian gathering in the first centuries. The fact that Aquila and Priscilla hosted house churches both in Ephesus (1 Cor 16:19) and in Rome (Rom 16:5) shows that they had sufficient resources and a central position in early Christian networks.

Pontus, Aquila's hometown, was a region on the southern coast of the Black Sea in northern Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey). The area had a significant Jewish population, and Jews from Pontus are also mentioned among the listeners on Pentecost (Acts 2:9).

The tentmaking trade (Greek: skēnopoios) shared by Aquila and Paul likely involved work with leather or weaving of Cilician goat-hair fabric. Shared craftsmanship was an important social link in the ancient world, and this common occupation laid the foundation for close cooperation between Paul and the couple.

Aquila and Priscilla are mentioned six times in the New Testament (Acts 18:2, 18, 26; Rom 16:3; 1 Cor 16:19; 2 Tim 4:19), making them one of the best-documented couples in the early church and testifying to their enduring significance in missionary work.
